sentences.text: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus grew to approximately 12 meters in length and weighed between 5 and 7 metric tons, ranking it among the largest known theropods.
Its jaws held sharp, recurved, and serrated teeth that resembled those of the great white shark, a feature that inspired the genus name.
The animal possessed one of the largest skulls observed in terrestrial animals, measuring approximately 1.60 meters in length.
These serrated teeth functioned to tear flesh, causing prey to bleed out.
A partial skeleton was discovered in Egypt in 1914 by crews working for Ernst Stromer, who formally reported the find in 1931.
This partial skeleton was first found near Ain Gedid, Egypt, in April 1914 by Richard Markgraf.
Separately, two teeth were unearthed in 1924 from wall cuts near Timimoun in French Algeria.
In 1925, Depéret and Savornin described these teeth as a new species, Megalosaurus saharicus.
Carcharodontosaurus was one of the largest known predatory dinosaurs and shared its territory and time with Spinosaurus, another large carnivorous dinosaur.
Estimates for the length and weight of C. saharicus range from 12 to 12.5 meters and 6 tons, respectively.
The genus Carcharodontosaurus was established by Ernst Stromer in 1931.
Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
The family Carcharodontosauridae was originally created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, but the name was not used until the late 20th century.
Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues defined the group Carcharodontosauridae in 2004 as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than to Allosaurus or Sinraptor.
Carcharodontosaurus fossils range from the Early to Late Cretaceous.

Carcharodontosaurus lived in the middle of the Cretaceous period, approximately 100 million years ago, between the Albian and Cenomanian stages, extending a few thousand years into the early Turonian, in what is now Africa.
The type skull was found in Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation in southeastern Morocco.
Fossils of C. iguidensis were found in the Echkar Formation near Iguidi, Niger.
Many fossils from French expeditions in North Africa were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on limited information, a classification now questioned.
A 2012 study suggests all isolated teeth previously assigned to Carcharodontosaurus from North Africa are indeterminate due to the presence of other genera in the region.
It is debated whether postcranial fossils from the Elrhaz Formation belong to Carcharodontosaurus or a different taxon, as the postorbital resembles Acrocanthosaurus.
Teeth from the Gara Samani Formation were identified as Carcharodontosaurus but may instead belong to abelisaurids.
